steps.caption: **Fixation** comes first. It preserves the tissue and stops autolysis, and poor fixation can't be corrected at any later step. Routine fixative is 10% neutral buffered formalin, at about 10–20 times the tissue's volume.

Paraffin won't mix with water or alcohol. So **dehydration** removes water through graded alcohols, then **clearing** in xylene removes the alcohol (dealcoholization) and makes the tissue translucent.
In **infiltration (impregnation)**, molten paraffin replaces the xylene and fills the tissue. In **embedding (blocking)**, the tissue is oriented in a mold of paraffin that sets into a block.
The block is **trimmed** to expose the tissue, then cut on a **rotary microtome**, the routine microtome for paraffin, into a ribbon of sections about 4–6 µm thick.

The ribbon is **floated out** on a warm water bath, kept a few degrees (about 6–10 °C) below the wax's melting point, to flatten. It is then **mounted** on a slide and dried. Clearing the bath between blocks stops tissue carry-over (floaters).
The section is dewaxed, rehydrated and **stained** (routinely H&E), then dehydrated, cleared and **coverslipped** with a mounting medium.
**The whole route:** fix → dehydrate → clear → infiltrate → embed → section → float and mount → stain → coverslip. Each fluid must mix with the one before it.

visuals.alt: A vertical flow of nine steps from specimen to slide: fixation in 10% neutral buffered formalin at 10–20 times the tissue volume, dehydration in graded alcohols, clearing in xylene, infiltration with molten paraffin, embedding in a mold, trimming and sectioning at 4–6 micrometres on a rotary microtome, floating out on a water bath kept about 6–10 °C below the wax melting point and mounting on a slide, staining, and coverslipping. A side panel gives each step's purpose and a classic error, and the last step explains that each fluid must mix with the one before it: water, alcohol, xylene, paraffin.
visuals.source: Original diagram. Facts per Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques; Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (fixation and tissue processing chapters).

steps.caption: Wax keeps out water-based dyes, so the section is first **deparaffinized** in xylene, then **hydrated** through descending alcohols to water.
In the **regressive** method, the section is deliberately **overstained** with hematoxylin (e.g. Harris). Nuclei are dark, and the cytoplasm holds excess dye too.
**Differentiation** in acid alcohol (e.g. 1% HCl in 70% alcohol) removes the excess dye, checked under the microscope, until only nuclei stay stained. In the acid they look reddish.
**Bluing** in a weak alkali, such as running tap water, Scott's tap water substitute or dilute ammonia water, turns the nuclear hematoxylin from red to an insoluble **blue**.
**Eosin**, an acid dye, counterstains the cytoplasm, collagen and red cells in shades of **pink** to red.
Finally the section is **dehydrated** through alcohols (which also differentiate the eosin), **cleared** in xylene and **mounted** under a coverslip in a resinous medium.

**Progressive** staining stops when the dye reaches the right intensity, so there is **no differentiation** step. **Regressive** staining overstains, then differentiates. Either way, the nuclei end up blue and the cytoplasm pink.

visuals.alt: A vertical flow of regressive H&E staining: dewax in xylene and hydrate through alcohols to water; overstain with hematoxylin; differentiate in acid alcohol; blue in alkaline water; counterstain with eosin; dehydrate in alcohols and clear in xylene; mount under a coverslip. A drawn cell beside the flow changes colour at each step: unstained, then a dark purple nucleus with excess dye in the cytoplasm, then a reddish nucleus with clear cytoplasm, then a blue nucleus, then pink cytoplasm. A final comparison shows that regressive staining is overstain, differentiate, blue, while progressive staining stains just to the endpoint with no differentiation, then blues.
visuals.source: Original diagram. Facts per Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques; Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (haematoxylin and eosin chapter).

steps.caption: The **Papanicolaou (Pap) stain** uses one nuclear stain and two cytoplasmic counterstains, applied in this order. The smear is first fixed wet in 95% ethyl alcohol.
**Hematoxylin** (commonly Harris) stains the **nuclei** blue to blue-black, showing the chromatin detail used to judge each cell.
**OG-6**, made with **orange G**, stains **keratinized** cytoplasm **orange**.
**EA** traditionally mixes three dyes. **Eosin Y** stains the cytoplasm of mature **superficial** squamous cells **pink**. It also colours nucleoli, cilia and red cells.
**Light green SF** (yellowish) stains the more metabolically active **intermediate** and **parabasal** cells **blue-green**. **Bismarck brown** adds little colour, and some EA formulas leave it out.
**Pap stain in one line:** hematoxylin → nuclei; OG-6 → keratin orange; EA → superficial cells pink (eosin Y) and intermediate and parabasal cells blue-green (light green SF).

visuals.alt: Three Pap stain solutions in order: 1 hematoxylin, the nuclear stain; 2 OG-6, made with orange G; 3 EA, eosin azure, containing eosin Y, light green SF and Bismarck brown. Four squamous cells are coloured step by step: all nuclei blue to blue-black with hematoxylin; a keratinized cell orange with OG-6; a superficial cell pink with eosin Y; and an intermediate cell and a parabasal cell blue-green with light green SF.
visuals.source: Original diagram. Facts per Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques; Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (cytology chapter, Papanicolaou method).

steps.caption: **Virchow:** organs are removed **one by one** and examined separately. It's simple, but the natural connections between organs are lost.
**Rokitansky:** organs are dissected **in situ**, opened and examined mostly in place inside the body, with little removed.

**Ghon:** organs are removed **en bloc**, in organ-system blocks: usually the neck and chest organs, the abdominal organs, and the urogenital system. Connections within each system are kept. Some texts take out the intestines as a separate block.

**Letulle:** the neck, chest, abdominal and pelvic organs are removed together **en masse**, as one mass, and dissected outside the body. It keeps the most connections, but the mass is bulky to handle.
**To remember:** Virchow = one by one; Rokitansky = in situ; Ghon = en bloc (organ blocks); Letulle = en masse (everything at once).

visuals.alt: A schematic body with its organs (neck organs, lungs, heart, liver, stomach, intestines, kidneys, bladder) beside a panel showing what comes out in each autopsy method. Virchow: each organ removed separately. Rokitansky: organs stay in the body and are dissected in situ. Ghon: organs removed en bloc in three blocks (neck and chest, abdominal, urogenital); some texts remove the intestines separately. Letulle: all organs removed together en masse as one mass and dissected outside the body. Cards along the bottom name each method and its key phrase.

steps.caption: **Plan:** define the problem, measure where you are now (the baseline), find the root cause, and plan a change with a measurable target.
**Do:** carry out the change, ideally as a small trial first, and collect data while it runs.
**Check:** compare the results with the baseline and the target to see whether the change worked. (Also called **Study**, in PDSA.)
**Act:** if the change worked, standardize it (update the SOP and train staff). If not, adjust it. Either way the cycle starts again.

**Quality control (QC)** checks each analytic run, e.g. a known positive control slide with a special stain. **Quality assurance (QA)** covers every phase. A mislabeled specimen is a pre-analytic error that QC can't catch, so QA uses PDCA to fix it.
**To remember:** Plan → Do → Check → Act, then repeat. PDCA is how a lab keeps improving quality over time.

visuals.alt: A cycle of four boxes joined by clockwise arrows: Plan (plan the fix), Do (try it on a small scale), Check (measure), Act (standardize), then repeat. A panel walks through reducing mislabeled specimens at each phase: measure the baseline and plan bedside labelling with two identifiers; pilot it on one ward; compare the new rate with the baseline and target; standardize in the SOP or adjust and repeat. Another panel shows quality assurance spanning the pre-analytic, analytic and post-analytic phases, with quality control (a control slide with each run) inside the analytic phase, and a mislabeled specimen in the pre-analytic phase.
